A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so people can load pages faster. Normally, a website lives on one machine called the origin server, the original computer that holds the real, master copy of everything. If everyone on Earth had to fetch data from that single machine, requests from far away would take longer to arrive. A CDN solves this by placing copies of the website on servers closer to visitors, called edge locations because they sit at the edge of the network, nearer to homes and offices rather than in one distant hub. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to hand over, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer came quickly from a nearby copy instead of a long trip to the origin. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of a popular book instead of everyone traveling to one national archive. Because most requests get served locally, pages load faster, the origin server faces less strain, and service keeps working even if traffic suddenly spikes. This is why streaming, shopping, and news sites all rely on CDNs during busy moments, like a product launch or a major sports event.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, master version of a website | Everything ultimately comes from here if no copy exists elsewhere |
| Edge location | A server placed close to everyday users, in many different regions | Shortens the distance data must travel, speeding up delivery |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy already answers a request | Avoids a long trip back to the origin, saving time |
| CDN | A network connecting many edge locations together | Spreads traffic out, preventing slowdowns and crashes |
